sections.html:
• Name: Xiphophorus pygmaeus
  • Other names: Dwarf Swordtail, Slender Pygmy Swordtail
  • Water type: freshwater
  • Minimum tank size: 10 gallons (~40 litres)
  • Keeping: medium
  • Breeding: easy to medium
  • Size: 1–1.6 inches (2.5–4 cm)
  • Optimal temperature: 71–78°F (22–26°C)
  • Optimal pH: 7.0–8.0
  • Optimal GH: 8–20
  • Dwellers: top and middle
  • Nitrate: less than 80
  • Diet: omnivore
  • Temperament: peaceful
  • Life span: up to 5 years
  • Colour forms: yellow, blue

Xiphophorus pygmaeus is a freshwater species endemic to Mexico and occurs exclusively in the Rio Axtla and its tributaries (Rio Tancuilin and Rio Huichihuayan) within the Pánuco River system.

According to the studies, this species is abundant in Rio Huichihuayan, less common in the lower 9 km of Rio Tancuilin and the upper 5 km of Rio Axtla.

These fish inhabit clear, shallow waters (less than 3 feet or 1 m deep), within well-shaded and moderately to fast-flowing spring-fed streams. They prefer undercut banks and dense stands of submerged aquatic vegetation.

Despite their small size, a group of 6–8 fish will require an absolute minimum aquarium size of 10 gallons (40 litres). Reasons include:

  • These fish are quite active and move around a lot.
  • If you have several males, there will be aggression because of limited space.
  • It is hard to create a current in small tanks.
  • Maintaining water balance and parameters is easier in larger aquariums because they hold a larger volume of water.
  • This allows for more stable water conditions and dilutes any potential fluctuations in water chemistry.

Important: Pygmy Swordtails are jumpers! Take measures such as using a tank cover, lowering the water level and using floating plants to ensure their safety.

Temperature: 71–78°F (22–26°C).

pH: these fish prefer slightly alkaline conditions. The ideal pH range is 7.0–8.0.

Hardness: the recommended general hardness (GH) range is 8 to 20 dGH. They do not like soft water.

Pygmy Swordtails are quite delicate fish. They are particularly sensitive to ammonia, nitrites and nitrates. It is therefore highly recommended to avoid introducing them as the first inhabitants immediately after the aquarium has finished cycling; wait at least a few weeks to allow a stable, balanced environment to establish.

Lighting

Pygmy Swordtails thrive in subdued lighting. However, if kept in planted tanks, lighting should be adapted to the needs of the plants.

Water flow

In their natural habitat, Pygmy Swordtails inhabit shallow waters where the current is moderate or relatively fast, and they like to swim in it. Although it is possible to keep these fish in an aquarium without a current, it is still advised to create one if you want to offer ideal conditions.

Aeration

Aeration and water flow often go hand in hand. A powerful filtration system needs to be in place to properly aerate the water and maintain a high level of oxygenation. The fish enjoy water rich in oxygen. Air stones and other aeration decor can be added for more oxygenation.

Decorations and plants

Pygmy Swordtails are shy and appreciate plenty of hiding places, such as caves, driftwood, tall plants and floating plants. They may retreat to these if they feel threatened or stressed.

It is not recommended to keep them in open aquariums; an open layout is unsettling for these timid fish.

Dwarf water lettuce, frogbit, duckweed and other floating plants are excellent at dimming light and providing the lighting these fish prefer.

This species is a diurnal omnivore. Pygmy Swordtails are not picky eaters; they will happily consume dry and freeze-dried foods such as flakes, pellets and crisps, as long as they suit their mouth size.

In the aquarium they can be fed a wide variety of foods such as:

  • spirulina
  • brine shrimp (Artemia salina)
  • Artemia nauplii
  • daphnia
  • fruit flies
  • moina
  • detritus worms
  • vinegar eels
  • mosquito larvae
  • cyclops, etc.

How to feed

This is a diurnal species, so it is better to feed them in the morning. Use the “five-minute rule”.

Ideally, feed in small portions (at least 2 times a day) rather than a large amount once a day. This mimics their natural feeding behaviour and helps prevent overfeeding and digestive issues.

  • Diet type: omnivore
  • Food preference: meat
  • Feeding frequency: daily

Are they plant safe?

Yes, Pygmy Swordtails are completely plant safe. They will not eat any healthy plants in the tank and do not eat living plant material.

Temper

Pygmy Swordtails are peaceful fish. Although males establish dominance hierarchies and compete for access to females, their agonistic interactions almost never escalate into physical contact.

It is generally recommended to keep only one male with several females, or a group of males with plenty of space and hiding places to reduce such behaviour.

Unlike their larger cousins, even when stressed they usually do not nip the fins of long-finned or slow-moving fish. They are quite shy and easily scared.

Activity

Pygmy Swordtails are relatively active and lively if there are no fish that can bully them. They enjoy exploring and are particularly fond of areas with dense vegetation or places to hide.

They are also good jumpers, so cover the tank or lower the water level by at least a few inches.

Sociality

Swordtails are social fish. It is recommended to keep them in groups of at least 3–4 individuals to ensure their well-being and encourage natural behaviour. Ideally, keep at least 3–4 females per male.

Being in a group allows natural behaviours, which reduces stress and improves overall well-being.

Do not introduce just a pair (male and female) into a tank. The female would be constantly harassed and pursued by the male, which exhausts, stresses and weakens her.

Placement in the tank

Pygmy Swordtails tend to occupy the upper and middle sections of the tank, with occasional visits to the bottom, which they don’t particularly favour.

  • Social: yes
  • Activity: moderate
  • Placement: top and middle dwellers
  • Peaceful: yes
  • Fin nippers: no
  • Jumpers: yes

placeholder

Breeding Pygmy Swordtails is relatively easy, similar to other livebearers. For breeding, keep a ratio of 1 male to 3–4 females.

Maturity

This species reaches maturity at around 5–6 months of age.

  • Males are considered mature when the gonopodium is fully formed (third, fourth and fifth anal fin rays elongated and fused) and the pectoral fins are fully pointed.
  • Females can be identified by a brood spot.

Mating

  • In this species there is no courtship. Even abnormally large males show only chasing behaviour. A male performs a parallel approach, swimming closely parallel to the female.
  • According to a study, with lower predation risk, females showed mating preferences for blue males, but yellow males dominated in agonistic interactions and were more aggressive in pursuing females. Females from populations with high predation risk showed no preference for blue males.
  • There is no sexual selection by females.
  • Females also prefer the large courting males of Xiphophorus nigrensis to their own small, non-courting males. Given a chance, females prefer larger conspecifics to small ones.
  • Xiphophorus pygmaeus can easily hybridize and produce viable offspring with other Xiphophorus species (such as X. cortezi and X. nigrensis).

Fertilization

Fertilization is internal. Males use a sexual organ called a gonopodium to introduce sperm into the female’s oviduct.

Gestation

Depending on the temperature, the gestation period is 3–4 weeks.

Fecundity

Xiphophorus pygmaeus is not a prolific breeder as some sources say, probably because of its small size and relatively large fry. On average, females give birth to only 3–4 fry.

Fry

Newborn fry are quite large (0.24–0.28 in or 6–7 mm). They require microscopic food such as infusoria, moina, artemia, or specialized liquid or powdered products.

In the wild, they almost never see their offspring, as the fry are immediately swept away by the current.

In aquariums the parents may mistake the fry for food, but this species will not deliberately hunt down and chase them, so in most cases the fry survive. To ensure survival, the aquarium should be densely planted or the fry should stay in a separate tank for at least a month.

Etymology

The genus name “Xiphophorus” is derived from two Greek words: “Xiphos”, meaning “Sword”, and “Phoros” meaning “Bearer or Carrier”. The species name “Pygmaeus” is of Greek origin, meaning “Dwarf or tiny”.

In 1943, Xiphophorus pygmaeus received its name because, during its description by Hubbs and Gordon, all known males of this species were observed to be smaller than males of closely related swordtail species.

Description

The Pygmy Swordtail is a very small freshwater fish belonging to the family Poeciliidae. The typical adult size ranges from 1 to 1.5 inches (2.5 to 3.8 cm).

Size: males average approximately 1 to 1.2 inches (2.5 to 3 cm). In rare cases males can reach almost 1.4 inches (3.8 cm), but these are exceptions, as experiments have shown that they do not pass on the gene responsible for size to their offspring. Females are slightly larger, on average 1.2 to 1.5 inches (29–40 mm). Xiphophorus continens and Xiphophorus multilineatus are also classified as smaller swordtails.

Coloration: the main coloration is greyish-brown, with a lighter belly. There are no vertical bars. Females often have one bold lateral line running from the eye along the body.

Colour genotypes: there are two genotypes of males, yellow and blue. They are called “blue” only by convention, because their colour is not actually blue but has brown nuances (the wild colour). Among the yellowish ones there can also be brightly coloured individuals, so some researchers consider them a third type, but this has not yet been recorded in scientific literature. Females are duller blue-gray with a yellow tint on the dorsal side.

Swords: Xiphophorus pygmaeus has a highly reduced sword or none. Most males do not exhibit a prominent sword; only a smaller proportion do. At the base of the caudal fin there can be a very short sword, generally less than 0.08 inches (2 mm) and never more than 0.3 inches (8 mm). The sword has no black edging.

Fins: the dorsal fin is relatively small, both in height and in length at the base. It is transparent, with a subtle black border and a faint black stripe that runs one-third of the way up the fin.

Lifespan

There is no data on the maximum lifespan in the wild. In aquariums, Pygmy Swordtails typically live 3–5 years if appropriately cared for. A suitable environment, a balanced diet and regular maintenance are important for their well-being and longevity.
